newsitem.title: RUSSIA: ARS says May 1 De Beers gem deal signing in doubt.
newsitem.headline: ARS says May 1 De Beers gem deal signing in doubt.

text.p: Russia's dominant diamond producer Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS) said on Monday that the May 1 target for the government go-ahead for a stalled gem deal with De Beers of South Africa may not be met.

"Unfortunately, what the government said before was not completely well-founded," said ARS spokesman Vladimir Logunov, when asked if the deal would be signed this week, as First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said recently.
"Chubais told a group of news editors on April 14 that no earlier than 10 days from then and no later than May 1 the agreement would be signed," Logunov said. "But where is he now?"
A deal between ARS and De Beers must be approved by the Russian government and authorised by a presidential decree before it comes into force.
Various Russian officials have been predicting the iminent approval of the deal for about six months and there is still no sign it will be approved by early May.
Logunov said the matter was further complicated by the fact that the government had yet to sign an order outlining diamond export quotas in 1997.
Officials at De Beers' Moscow office were not immediately available for comment.

De Beers, frustrated at Moscow's inability to communicate its position on a draft agreement submitted to the cabinet in October 1996, sharply curtailed its purchases of gems from Russia at the end of last year.

Logunov had said earlier that De Beers purchased rough gems from ARS during the first quarter of 1997, but that the company had been unable to export the gems because there were no export quotas in place.

Further sales of rough gems have been made to domestic diamond cutters and polishers during the first four months of this year, but gem stocks have risen nonetheless as a result of the absence of full trading relations between ARS and De Beers.

De Beers' London-based Central Selling Organisation controls about three quarters of the world's $4.5 billion-a-year trade in uncut diamonds, and Russia accounts for about 20 percent of annual CSO sales.
